summary.text:
A clean, well-reconciled treasury outturn from a council that is fundamentally a net investor. Our PWLB price book returns 4 loans totalling £23,344,146 at a weighted 2.6600%, all fixed-rate EIP — matching Table 3 of Appendix A to £6k on principal and to two decimals on rate, and matching the paper's own narrative that all borrowing is HRA self-financing from the 28 March 2012 tranche. One of the cleanest reconciliations we have run.

The balance-sheet identity ties exactly: Total CFR £28.00m less external borrowing £23.34m less other debt liabilities £3.53m = £1.13m internal borrowing, which is what the Council prints at Table 1. Only 4.6% of Loans CFR is carried internally — Dartford has essentially fully-externalised its HRA debt.

The scale of the picture is that investments are eight times debt: £186.48m against £23.34m. And the Council isn't borrowing — no new long-term debt in 2025/26, none in Q1 2026/27 either, and the liability benchmark is deeply negative every year of the forecast (−£153.14m at 31.3.26, still −£110.95m at 31.3.28) with the Arlingclose chart showing it stays below −£50m through 2074. Verbatim: 'the Council has no need to borrow for the foreseeable future'.

The other feature that stands out is proactive positioning against the 2029 statutory override cliff. Dartford has set aside a £9.81m investment volatility reserve — roughly 10% of the £97.68m strategic pooled book — and has decided to maintain it because the override may not be extended past 2029. That is one of the most proactive treatments of the 2029 cliff we have read; compare Chichester's £4m reserve on a £36.8m pooled book, or Broxtowe holding none.

Investment income £7.45m outperformed the £5.05m budget by £2.40m; the externally managed pooled funds delivered £4.55m of dividend income plus £4.88m of unrealised capital gain on top. Debt cost £0.67m for the year — the investment book pays 11× the debt cost. The report author on the covering paper is Davinder Sandhu (Financial Services); no S151 is named and no email address is printed anywhere in the four papers we hold. That is why this note is drafted but blocked on the recipient line.

officer.body:
Hi,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the Annual Treasury Report Cabinet noted on 23 July and Panel took on 28 July. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. The report is clear and well laid out and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

A cross-check first, which comes out unusually clean. Our PWLB price book holds 4 loans for Dartford totalling £23,344,146 at a weighted 2.6600%, all fixed-rate EIP. Your Table 3 on page 6 gives £23.35m at 2.66% over 8.53 years, with a note underneath that all the borrowing is for HRA self-financing and all fixed-rate EIP. That is a match on the count, on the principal to £6k, on the rate to the basis point, and on the shape of the book. Same story on both sides of the table. One of the cleanest reconciliations we've run.

The balance sheet ties too. CFR £28.00m less external borrowing £23.34m less £3.53m of IFRS 16 lease liabilities is £1.13m, which is exactly what your Table 1 on page 5 prints as internal over borrowing. Only 4.6% of your Loans CFR is carried internally — the HRA book is essentially fully externalised, and that's rare among the councils we've read.

The scale of the picture is what most caught our eye. £186.48m of treasury investments against £23.34m of external borrowing — an eight-to-one net-investor position — and your liability benchmark on page 13 is deeply negative every year of the forecast, starting at minus £153m at 31 March and still minus £111m by 31 March 2028. The Arlingclose chart on page 14 keeps it below minus £50m all the way to 2074. Your own paper puts it plainly: no need to borrow for the foreseeable future. That agrees with the Q1 update, which shows no new borrowing since April 2025 and the next £1.45m repayment landing on 1 August. So the PWLB story here isn't a borrowing story, it's a debt runoff story, and it runs through the late 2030s as the 2012 EIPs amortise down to zero. What that looks like priced against today's DMO curve is on your loan page at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

The other thing that stands out is on the investment side, and it's a positive one. The £9.81m investment volatility reserve you've set aside against the 2029 statutory override cliff, and the decision on page 10 to maintain it because the override may not be extended past 2029, is one of the most proactive treatments of the 2029 cliff we've read. Ten per cent coverage on a £97.68m strategic pooled book is well ahead of most councils we hold — where reserves either don't exist or are small fractions of the position. Not something we can add to. Worth naming so you know how it sits against the library.

The income line reads consistently with all of the above. £7.45m of GF Net Investment Income against a £5.05m budget, £4.55m of pooled-fund dividends and £4.88m of unrealised capital gain on top — the total return on your book is comfortably ahead of the income-only 4.02% that Table 5 compares to the 4.29% similar-LA benchmark, because that benchmark doesn't include the unrealised capital gain that sits behind the statutory override. That is one of those places where an income-only comparison understates you rather than the other way round.

On training, four look most relevant. Investment strategy for debt-free (and nearly-debt-free) councils speaks to your shape directly. Liability Benchmark: the essentials is worth watching given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes and how far below zero yours already sits. IFRS 9 statutory override — the 2029 cliff sits alongside the £9.81m reserve you've already thought about. Members' introduction to treasury is written for Panel-level audiences. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
